name: Antakarinya
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

earlier_scan.note: Nearly extinct Wati (Pama-Nyungan); only classification (O'Grady & Voegelins 1966) and community history found; no grammar/phonology covering stress located.

new_statements.quote: There are two types of stress possible within a Yankunytjatjara word, both fully predictable. The auditory correlates of stress are relatively higher pitch and greater loudness. In decreasing order of prominence: (1) Primary stress normally occurs on the initial vowel of a word, and on the initial vowel of reduplicated roots. Directional prefixes to verbs behave as separate phonological words in that both prefix and verb receive primary stress. (2) Secondary stress is found on the initial vowel of di- and polymoric suffixes.
new_statements.citation: Goddard, Cliff. 1983. A semantically-oriented grammar of the Yankunytjatjara dialect of the Western Desert language. PhD thesis, Australian National University. (Published as Goddard 1985, A grammar of Yankunytjatjara, IAD, Alice Springs.)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable of every word (and of each reduplicated root or directional-prefix + verb unit); secondary stress on the first syllable of each disyllabic or longer suffix. Fully predictable. The same first-syllable rule, with secondary stress on the third syllable of longer words, is given for the Ooldea dialect by Douglas 1955 (via SPA 1979, p. 315) and for the Warburton Ranges dialect by Douglas 1958, Part One §3, p. 8.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Goddard 1983: on the initial vowel of di-/polymoric suffixes (morphologically conditioned, so the third syllable of a trimoric root gets no secondary stress). Douglas 1955/1958 (other Western Desert dialects): secondary stress generally on the third syllable in words of more than three syllables; hyphenated compounds take initial stress on each part.
new_statements.exceptions: Directional prefixes to verbs and reduplicated roots count as separate phonological words with their own primary stress; Goddard fn. 8 notes a potential minimal pair kutjupa-tjara vs kutjupatjara so stress is phonemic in classical terms though predictable from morphology. Douglas 1958: sentence stress (heavier) overrides on emphasised items and interrogative particles.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word); cited from analysis of Yankunytjatjara consultants aged 50+, mainly men, at Mimili/Indulkana/Fregon. NOT a description of Antikirinya proper: the thesis never mentions Antikirinya. Applicability to anta1253 rests on Naessan 2009 (TOC only) treating Antikirinya as an internal variant of Yankunytjatjara.
new_statements.identity_note: No opened source describes Antikirinya (anta1253) itself. The quoted statement is Goddard 1983 on Yankunytjatjara (Glottolog yank1247), which Naessan 2009 (TOC, §4.7.2.4) treats as the language of which Antikirinya is an internal variant; Goddard's thesis never mentions Antikirinya. sources.quote: There are two types of stress possible within a Yankunytjatjara word, both fully predictable. The auditory correlates of stress are relatively higher pitch and greater loudness. In decreasing order of prominence: (1) Primary stress normally occurs on the initial vowel of a word, and on the initial vowel of reduplicated roots. Directional prefixes to verbs behave as separate phonological words in that both prefix and verb receive primary stress. sources.note: §2.2.3 Stress, p. 27: two fully predictable stress types; primary stress on the initial vowel of a word and of reduplicated roots (directional prefixes to verbs are separate phonological words, each with primary stress); secondary stress on the initial vowel of di-/polymoric suffixes; fn. 8 notes stress is phonemic in classical-phonemic terms though morphemically predictable. Describes Yankunytjatjara (Mimili/Indulkana/Fregon consultants); the word Antikirinya does not occur in the thesis.

sources.note: p. 315, STRESS field quoting Douglas 1955 (Oceania 25, p. 222): 'Syllable stress... [is] predictable [and] non-phonemic. When unaffected by heavier intonational [= sentence] stress, syllable stress falls on the first syllable of each word. In words of more than three syllables a secondary stress generally falls on the third syllable.... Interrogative particles always carry sentence stress.' sources.citation: Douglas, W. H. 1958. An introduction to the Western Desert language. Oceania Linguistic Monographs 4. Part One: Pronunciation (Warburton Ranges dialect). Rosetta Project excerpt on archive.org.
sources.note: Part One §3 'Stress or accent', p. 8: 'The FIRST syllable of each word is stressed (or accented). E.g. kutjara two is pronounced ku-tjara. In words of more than three syllables the primary stress is still on the first syllable, but a secondary stress generally falls on the third syllable'; compounds hyphenated, each part takes initial stress; sentence stress on emphasised items and interrogatives. Describes the Warburton Ranges (Ngaanyatjarra) dialect, not Antikirinya.
